categories.title: Healthcare
categories.intro: Get private health insurance first, because you need it for the visa. After about 3 months of living there, apply for the French state cover (PUMa) and the carte Vitale. Then decide what to do about US Medicare.
categories.saintMartinDiffers: Saint-Martin has no CPAM of its own. Health cover is run by the CGSS of Guadeloupe, which has a front desk at Spring Concordia in Marigot. Files go to its postal address in Les Abymes (Guadeloupe).

items.title: Get health insurance quote A (international plan)
steps: Write down the age of each person to cover and your arrival date.
Contact one international health insurer that covers people living in French Saint-Martin.
Ask for a yearly price in euros for everyone to be covered.
Ask if it covers doctor visits, specialists, prescriptions, hospital stays and evacuation.
Ask how it handles health conditions you already have.
Save the quote as a PDF in the app's notes.
items.source: service-public.fr F302 (health insurance is required for the visiteur status)

items.title: Get health insurance quote B (second insurer, same questions)
steps: Contact a second insurer.
Ask the same questions you asked for quote A.
Put both quotes side by side: yearly price, deductible, area covered, evacuation.
Pick one.

items.title: Read the rules on health conditions you already have
steps: Open the policy wording for the plan you picked.
Find the section on 'pre-existing conditions'.
Write down any waiting period or anything that is not covered.
If something matters to you, ask the insurer to confirm it by email.
items.source: Named source: the insurer's policy wording
items.sourceNote: No official page for this step; confirm with the named provider.

items.title: Ask the insurer for a certificate written for the visa
steps: Ask the insurer for an 'attestation d'assurance' in French or English.
Check it shows every insured name, start and end dates, and that it covers the whole stay.
Check it covers Saint-Martin (French side).
Check the amounts are shown in euros.
Save the PDF and print one copy for the visa folder.

items.title: Set the policy to start on the day you arrive
steps: Tell the insurer your flight date.
Ask them to start the policy that day, not later.
If you have travel insurance for the trip, check it ends after the new policy starts.
items.sourceNote: No official page for this step; confirm with the named provider.

items.title: Decide on medical evacuation cover (yes or no)
steps: Check if your health plan already includes evacuation.
If not, get one price for an evacuation membership.
Decide and write the answer in notes.
items.sourceNote: No official page for this step; confirm with the named provider.

items.title: Do doctor, dentist and eye check-ups before you leave
steps: Book appointments with your current doctor, dentist and eye doctor.
Ask each office for a copy of your records and recent test results.
Save the copies in the cloud and keep paper copies in your carry-on.
items.sourceNote: No official page for this step; confirm with the named provider.

items.title: Store your insurance card and policy offline
steps: Download the policy, the card and the claims phone number.
Save them on every phone so they open without internet.
Print one copy for the document bag.

items.title: Compare top-up cover (mutuelle)
items.phase: After you arrive: French state cover (PUMa)
steps: PUMa pays only part of most bills. A mutuelle pays some or all of the rest.
Ask 2 insurers in Saint-Martin for a mutuelle price for everyone in the household.
If your income is low, read about the Complémentaire santé solidaire (free or low-cost top-up).
Decide if you keep your international plan, switch to a mutuelle, or keep both for a while.

items.title: Save the hospital and emergency numbers
items.phase: After you arrive: French state cover (PUMa)
steps: Save the Louis-Constant Fleming hospital (Spring Concordia) in every phone.

Find the nearest pharmacy to your home.

items.title: Read what Medicare covers outside the US
steps: Open the Medicare.gov page 'Travel outside the U.S.'.
Note the main point: Medicare usually does not pay for care outside the US.
This applies only to someone who has Medicare or will soon.

items.title: Decide: keep or drop Medicare Part B
steps: Part A is usually free, so most people keep it.
Part B has a monthly premium even if you live abroad.
If you drop Part B and sign up again later, you may pay a lifelong penalty and can only re-enroll in set periods.
Read the penalty page, then decide. Write the decision and date in notes.

links.label: Medicare.gov: When you can sign up

items.source: Medicare.gov: late enrollment penalties; sign-up periods
items.verify: Ask SSA or Medicare your exact penalty and re-enrollment dates before you cancel anything.

items.title: Check any Medicare Advantage, Part D or Medigap plan
steps: List any extra Medicare plan you pay for.
Call each plan and ask what happens when you move out of the US.
Most of these plans need a US service area. Write the answer in notes.
items.source: Medicare.gov; named source: each plan's member services
items.verify: Each plan's own rules for members who move abroad.

categories.title: Banking
categories.intro: Keep your home bank working from abroad, then open a French euro account once you have an address. US citizens: banks will ask for a US tax form (FATCA), and you report foreign accounts to the US each year.
categories.saintMartinDiffers: Saint-Martin uses the euro and SEPA transfers like mainland France. If a bank refuses you, the 'right to an account' goes through IEDOM (its Guadeloupe office covers Saint-Martin), not the Banque de France.

items.title: Ask your home bank if you can keep the account while living abroad
steps: Call your main bank at home.
Ask: 'Can I keep my checking account if I live in French Saint-Martin?'
Ask: 'Can I use a foreign address, or do you need a home-country address?'
Write the answer and the agent's name in notes.
items.sourceNote: No official page for this step; confirm with the named provider.
items.verify: Some banks (many in the US) close or limit accounts with a foreign address. Get the answer in writing if you can.

items.title: Turn on international use for your home-country cards
steps: Open your bank app.
Find the travel or international settings.
Turn on foreign use for each card.
Note any card that does not work abroad.
items.sourceNote: No official page for this step; confirm with the named provider.

items.title: Check which card has no foreign transaction fee
steps: Look at each card's fee list.
Find 'foreign transaction fee' and 'ATM fee'.
Pick one card with no foreign fee for daily use.
items.source: Named source: your card issuer's fee list
items.sourceNote: No official page for this step; confirm with the named provider.

items.title: Open a multi-currency account and send a small test
steps: Open an account with a multi-currency service (for example Wise).
Send a small amount in euros to yourself.
Check how long it took and what it cost.

items.title: Make sure bank sign-in does not depend only on your home-country SIM
steps: Set up an authenticator app where the bank allows it.
Save the backup codes in a safe place (not in this app).
Test one sign-in with your phone on Wi-Fi only.
items.source: Named source: your bank's security settings
items.sourceNote: No official page for this step; confirm with the named provider.

items.title: Make a shortlist of 2 or 3 banks in Saint-Martin
steps: List banks with a branch in Marigot or nearby.
Call or visit each one.
Ask: 'What do you need to open an account for a [your nationality] citizen?'
Ask if you need an appointment.
items.sourceNote: No official page for this step; confirm with the named provider.
items.verify: Which banks have branches open to new personal customers in Saint-Martin today.

items.title: US citizens: fill in the US tax form the bank will ask for (W-9)
steps: French banks must report US customers to the IRS (FATCA).
They will ask each of you for an IRS Form W-9 or their own self-certification form.
Fill it in at the bank. Your tax number goes on that form only, never in this app.

items.title: Put the bank document folder together
steps: Passport.
Visa or residence card.
Proof of address in Saint-Martin, less than 3 months old.
Proof of income (for example a pension or benefit letter).
US citizens only: the W-9 or the bank's own US self-certification form.
Any other form the bank lists.
items.source: Named source: the bank's own list
items.sourceNote: No official page for this step; confirm with the named provider.

items.title: Open the French account and get your RIB
steps: Go to the appointment with the folder.
Sign the account agreement.
Ask for your RIB (bank details sheet with your IBAN).
Save the RIB as a PDF. Many offices will ask for it.
items.sourceNote: No official page for this step; confirm with the named provider.

items.title: If a bank says no: use your 'right to an account'
steps: Ask the bank for a written refusal (attestation de refus).
If they do not answer within 15 days of a registered-letter request, that counts as a refusal.
Fill in the IEDOM 'droit au compte' form.
Send it online or hand it in at IEDOM with your ID and a proof of address less than 3 months old.
IEDOM names a bank that must open a basic account for you.

links.label: IEDOM: Your right to a bank account

items.saintMartinDiff: In mainland France this goes through the Banque de France. In Saint-Martin it goes through IEDOM.

items.title: Agree with the landlord how you will pay rent
steps: Ask if they want a SEPA transfer or a direct debit.
Get their IBAN in writing.
Set up the first payment from your French account.

items.title: Learn the FBAR rule for foreign accounts
items.phase: US citizens: reporting to the US each year
steps: If all your foreign accounts together go over $10,000 at any time in the year, you must file an FBAR.
It is filed online with FinCEN, not with your tax return.
Put a yearly reminder for April 15 (there is an automatic extension to October 15).

links.label: FinCEN BSA E-Filing (where the FBAR is filed)

items.estTime: 15 min to learn; 30 min a year to file
items.verify: Confirm the current deadline on the IRS FBAR page each year.

items.title: Check if you must also file Form 8938
items.phase: US citizens: reporting to the US each year
steps: Form 8938 is filed with your US tax return.
The amounts that trigger it are higher for people living abroad.
Open the IRS page and check the table for 'taxpayers living abroad'.
Ask your tax preparer to confirm.

items.title: Check both passports
steps: Find the expiry date on each passport.
It must be valid at least 3 months after your visa ends.
It must have 2 blank pages and be less than 10 years old.

categories.title: Income, Social Security and taxes
categories.intro: Make sure any pension or benefit from home keeps paying you abroad, and know which tax office you answer to. Saint-Martin has its own income tax, separate from mainland France, and tax treaties signed by France may not cover it (for US citizens, the US-France treaty).
categories.saintMartinDiffers: Saint-Martin sets and collects its own income tax. Returns go to the Centre des finances publiques in Concordia, due May 31. The '5-year rule' is aimed at people coming from mainland France or a French DOM. The US-France treaty defines France as the European and overseas departments, and Saint-Martin stopped being part of a department in 2007.

items.title: Ask your preparer if the US-France treaty covers Saint-Martin
steps: The treaty defines France as the European and overseas departments.
Saint-Martin has been a separate collectivity, not a department, since 2007.
Ask your preparer what that means for your Social Security and other income.
Write the answer in notes.

items.title: Learn about the US foreign tax credit
steps: If Saint-Martin taxes your income, you may be able to subtract that from your US tax.
This uses IRS Form 1116.

steps: You still file a US return every year.
Living abroad gives an automatic 2-month extension to June 15 to file.
Any tax owed is still due April 15, or interest is charged.

categories.title: Immigration and the préfecture
categories.intro: If you are not an EU/EEA/Swiss citizen, apply for a long-stay visa for Saint-Martin from your country of residence before you move. For people who will not work, this is usually the 'visiteur' visa. After you arrive, validate it online if it is a VLS-TS, then renew through the préfecture in Concordia.
categories.saintMartinDiffers: Saint-Martin is outside the Schengen area. The visa must name Saint-Martin (or 'DFA'). A visa for mainland France does not cover it. You land at SXM on the Dutch side, where there is no French border check. The préfecture is shared with Saint-Barthélemy and sits in Concordia, Marigot.

items.title: Decide together: long-stay visa or short visits
steps: Many nationalities, including US citizens, can visit for up to 90 days in any 180 days without a visa. Check yours in the France-Visas wizard.

categories.title: Vehicle, driving licence and insurance
categories.intro: Drive a rental at first. A non-EU licence works for 1 year after you become residents, then you must swap it at the Collectivité. Buying a car locally is usually simpler than shipping one.

categories.intro: Who to call in an emergency, and how your government can reach you.
categories.saintMartinDiffers: For US citizens, consular help for French Saint-Martin comes from the US Embassy in Bridgetown, Barbados, not the US Consulate in Curaçao that covers Sint Maarten.

items.title: Save French emergency numbers
steps: 15 medical, 17 police, 18 fire, 112 any emergency.
Save them in every phone.

items.title: Sign up for your government's travel alerts (US: STEP)
steps: US citizens: go to the State Department's STEP site.
Create an account and add your Saint-Martin address.
You will get safety and storm alerts.
